**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject scalar stores sourced from vec4 loads**

When a scalar `fpow`/`fdiv` stores only the `.x` result of two vec4 SSBO loads, this new predicate records `value_components == 1` because `unary_alu_src_is_identity_load(..., components=1)` only checks swizzle lane 0 and the code above only requires the two loads to match each other, not the scalar carrier width. The replay path then selects `PIPE_FORMAT_R32_FLOAT` for both inputs (checked via `rg --fixed-strings r300vk_binary_transcendental_dispatch_replay src/`), so gid 1 samples byte 4 rather than the next vec4 element at byte 16, silently corrupting scalar outputs derived from vector inputs; require the load component counts/stride to match the scalar carrier or reject this shape.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject non-canonical bitwise SSBO offsets**

When a bitwise kernel uses anything other than the same per-invocation offset for both loads and the store (for example `out[gid] = a[gid] & b[gid + 1]`, or the constant-offset shape used by the new unit builder), this detector still marks the pipeline as `is_bitwise_logicop` because it only checks that the store value is an ALU of the two load defs. The replay path ignores the NIR offsets and always maps texel `i` to `a[i] OP b[i]` and writes `out[i]`, so these admitted kernels silently produce different results instead of falling through to the no-op/unknown-shape path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Distinguish captured binding 0 from missing bindings**

For a valid in-place bitwise kernel whose two `load_ssbo`s and `store_ssbo` all use descriptor binding 0, the detector records `{0,0,0}`, but this replay treats that as the sentinel for “bindings were not captured” and falls back to the first three storage-buffer bindings. With a single-buffer layout this makes the dispatch no-op, and with extra storage buffers it resolves the wrong input/output descriptors; the pattern needs explicit binding-valid state instead of using zero as missing.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject conditional bitwise stores**

When the single bitwise `store_ssbo` is guarded by a `nir_if` or another predicate, the flat walk still records it and sets `is_bitwise_logicop`, but the replay path always draws a fullscreen quad and writes every invocation. In that conditional-store shape, lanes where the shader should leave the destination untouched are overwritten with `a OP b`, so the detector needs to reject or separately model control flow before enabling this replay.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Require scalar loads for scalar shift replay**

For a kernel that loads a `uvec2`/`uvec4` SSBO element and stores only one shifted lane, `unary_alu_src_is_identity_load()` can still match the vector load through the ALU swizzle, while this guard only verifies the scalar store/result. The replay then wraps the input as one RGBA8 texel per invocation (4-byte stride), but the source load's element offset can advance by the vector element size (for example 16 bytes for `uvec4`), so gid > 0 samples the wrong bytes and writes incorrect shift results. Please also require the matched `load_ssbo` def to be scalar 32-bit before setting `is_shift_logical`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve binding-zero in-place shift captures**

For an in-place logical-shift kernel on storage binding 0 when the descriptor set layout also contains another compute-visible storage buffer, both captured binding fields are zero, so this treats the detector result as uncaptured. The one-in/one-out fallback then resolves the first storage buffer as input and the second as output, so `buf0[i] <<= k` writes the shifted data to binding 1 instead of back to binding 0. The shift pattern needs binding-valid/in-place information, rather than using zero as both a valid binding and the uncaptured sentinel.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject shifted scatter/gather offsets**

When a shift kernel uses different supported load/store offsets, such as `out[gid + 1] = in[gid] << k`, this detector still marks it as a raster shift because it only checks the value def and not the load/store address relationship. The replay path writes one output texel at the raster index and cannot honor the NIR store offset, so these admitted scatter/gather variants silently write the shifted value to the wrong element; require semantic offset equivalence before setting `is_shift_logical`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Don't admit conditional shift stores**

For a shift store guarded by control flow that does not add another SSBO load, such as `if ((gid & 1) != 0) out[gid] = in[gid] << k`, this detector still sets `is_shift_logical` because it only counts one load and one store and never checks whether the store is inside a `nir_if`. The replay is an unconditional fullscreen write, so lanes where the predicate is false are overwritten instead of preserving the original output; require the store to be unconditional or route a predicated shift through a masked-store path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Mask variable shift amounts before LUT lookup**

For variable shifts where the loaded amount's low byte is 32..255, this feeds the raw byte into a 32-texel CLAMP lookup instead of using the NIR shift amount modulo 32; NIR defines `ishl`/`ushr` as shifting by `src1 & (sizeof(src0) * 8 - 1)` (src/compiler/nir/nir_opcodes.py:984-991, found with `rg --fixed-strings nir_op_ishl src/compiler/nir/`). For example, `b = 32` should behave like shift 0, but left shift samples texel 31 and right shift clamps to texel 0 before the fixed 31-bit window, producing the wrong result.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject vector loads in variable-shift detection**

When the shift operands come from vector `load_ssbo`s but only `.x` is shifted/stored, this check still accepts the shape as long as both loads have the same vector width. The replay path then wraps each input as one RGBA8 texel per invocation (4 bytes), so a source load that actually advances by 16 bytes for `uvec4` elements is replayed with scalar stride and reads later components/elements instead of the intended per-invocation values. Require the load component count to match the scalar store before marking this as `is_shift_variable`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve unrelated bytes on subrange shift writes**

For variable-shift outputs that are descriptor subranges or share a larger `VkBuffer` with other data, this helper now writes the result via `out_res` but still maps with `PIPE_MAP_DISCARD_WHOLE_RESOURCE`. That allows the driver to invalidate bytes outside `out_box` even though the shader only owns the descriptor range; other readback helpers in this file choose `DISCARD_RANGE` unless the write covers the whole resource. Use the same range-aware flags here so a variable-shift dispatch does not corrupt adjacent buffer contents.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve equal input bindings for variable shifts**

For kernels that use the same SSBO for the value and the shift amount, such as `out[gid] = buf[gid] << buf[gid]`, the detector legitimately records equal input bindings. This branch treats equality as a missing-binding sentinel and replaces the captured bindings with the first three storage buffers from the layout, so the dispatch either no-ops when only two buffers are bound or reads the amount from an unrelated second descriptor. Fall back only when the detector actually failed to capture bindings, not when the two operands intentionally alias.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve BA operand order when bindings are opaque**

When this detector is used from `r300vk_classify_compute_kernel`, SSBO binding sources have been lowered to descriptor handles, so these constant-only assignments do not fire; `r300vk_two_in_one_out_dispatch_replay` then sees all three captures as zero and falls back to positional layout order. In a real ba subtraction kernel—the optimizer-hoisted case this patch targets—replay still binds `input_a` to the first layout storage buffer instead of `op_lhs`, so the synthesized FS continues to compute the old reversed subtraction. Carry the `ba` swap into the opaque/fallback path as well, not only the constant-binding test path.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Use the target plane order for planar chroma**

When an application creates the decode target as `VA_FOURCC_YV12`/`PIPE_FORMAT_YV12` (advertised for YUV420 alongside IYUV), the three resources are ordered Y,V,U (`PIPE_FORMAT_YV12` is `Y8_V8_U8_420_UNORM`). This new planar branch treats every three-plane target as Y,U,V and maps `surfaces[1]` as Cb and `surfaces[2]` as Cr, so intra reconstruction swaps the chroma planes and produces wrong colors on YV12 surfaces. Please use the buffer format's plane order, or pass explicit Cb/Cr surfaces instead of assuming IYUV.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Don't skip planar chroma when plane strides differ**

For VA external-buffer or PRIME three-plane surfaces, U and V are imported with independent per-plane pitches, so their mapped transfer strides are not guaranteed to match. With this guard, any planar target whose Cb and Cr strides differ silently returns without reconstructing either chroma plane, leaving intra chroma at the previous/cleared contents even though both planes mapped successfully. Please handle separate Cb/Cr strides instead of treating unequal strides as a no-op.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Split source and destination chroma layout decisions**

This helper now accepts independent Cb/Cr source and destination views, but this flag derives the reference sampling mode from the destination surface. If the DPB reference and current target use different layouts (the VA H.264 path copies ReferenceFrames into `h264.ref` and only validates the target buffer format), a planar target with an NV12 reference passes a NULL `ref_chroma_cr` into `scale_copy`, while an NV12 target with a planar reference samples lane 1 of an R8 Cb view and reconstructs Cr from Cb. Use separate source/destination layout checks, or reject mismatched layouts before calling this helper.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Handle YV12 planar component order**

When a VA client creates H.264 decode surfaces with the YV12 pixel format, it maps to `PIPE_FORMAT_YV12` / `Y8_V8_U8_420`, so `get_sampler_view_planes()` and `get_surfaces()` expose plane 1 as Cr and plane 2 as Cb. This new inter path unconditionally treats `ref_planes[1]` and `target_surfaces[1]` as Cb and `[2]` as Cr, so P-frame chroma on YV12 surfaces is reconstructed from and written to the opposite component planes. Use the buffer format or plane order to choose the Cb/Cr indices instead of fixed planar indices.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve the drain streak until usage actually drops**

In the OOM scenario this is meant to contain, GTT can keep rising one 32 MiB budget at a time; after each drain, the next realloc usually falls below the new `gtt_drain_mark + budget` and takes this `else` arm, resetting `gtt_drain_streak` to zero even though usage has not fallen below the post-drain mark. That prevents the hard cap from ever reaching four for gradual unbounded growth, so the SW-TCL draw can still continue climbing toward host OOM instead of being dropped.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Do not reject an advertised uniform-texel-buffer feature**

This rejects any `GLSL_SAMPLER_DIM_BUF`, including uniform texel buffers, but `r300vk_physical_device.c` still advertises `VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_2_UNIFORM_TEXEL_BUFFER_BIT` for PIPE_BUFFER sampler-view formats. An app or deqp case that selects one of those advertised formats now gets `VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT` at pipeline creation, making the exposed uniform-texel-buffer support unusable; either stop advertising it or keep the rejection limited to descriptor types that are not exposed.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Remove host-specific tool paths from AGENTS**

The root AGENTS.md hard rule says checked-in files must use repository-relative paths, PATH-resolved tools, or explicit user roots and must not contain local absolute paths or per-user toolchains, but this new note records `/usr/bin/...` locations and `~/.local/bin` for one CachyOS/Arch setup. That makes the repository instructions host-specific and contradicts the policy in the same file; refer to PATH-resolved tool names or move these notes out of the tracked Mesa repo.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Scalarize vector constant masks before rejecting them**

When a shader uses a vector low-bit mask such as `uvec4(3)`, the iand is still FP24-exact per lane after scalarization, but this check rejects it solely because the backing load_const has multiple components. Those otherwise-lowerable vector bitfield idioms now set `compiler->Error` and get replaced by the dummy shader; inspect each ALU source component or scalarize before sending the op to the unsupported path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reset the GTT drop flag at an actual draw boundary**

This reset is in `get_vertex_info`, but the draw frontend is cached and a backend-only `draw_flush` after `r300_swtcl_draw_vbo` does not force `get_vertex_info` to run for the next draw with the same prim/opt. Once one large draw sets `gtt_budget_exceeded`, subsequent unrelated draws can keep returning early from `r300_render_draw_{arrays,elements}` until a state or primitive change rebuilds the frontend, so move this reset to a real per-draw boundary.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

When aliasing is detected, this promotes to a fresh allocation-sized owns buffer but does not preserve the current contents of the previously bound buffer(s). A later vkMapMemory (or a submit-boundary HOST_COHERENT sync while mapped) can therefore expose/copy undefined bytes instead of the existing device-visible contents that were in the evicted buffer slice.

The aliasing-promotion path appends an evicted slice using mem->memory_offset without validating that the previous binding's offset+size fits in the VkDeviceMemory allocation. If an invalid bind slips through the borrow path, this can later trip range errors during sync or lead to incorrect copies. Validate the evicted slice bounds before recording it.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict alias promotion to buffer resources**

When the same `VkDeviceMemory` was previously bound to an image, `BindImageMemory2` leaves `mem->resource` pointing at the image's `PIPE_TEXTURE_2D` resource. This new predicate treats any distinct resource as a buffer alias and records that texture in `bound_buffers`; the next unmap/flush/submit sync walks those slices via `r300vk_sync_one_buffer_slice`, which calls `buffer_map` on each slice, so a valid image-then-buffer alias can fail or corrupt synchronization instead of being handled separately. Guard this path to borrowed `PIPE_BUFFER` resources or add a separate image-alias path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Seed existing slices before switching to owned storage**

When a second buffer bind promotes an already-populated allocation while no map is live, this swaps in a fresh allocation-sized `owned` buffer without copying the evicted buffer's current bytes into it. Later, if the app maps a range that intersects the earlier slice, then unmaps or submits, the new host-to-buffer sync uses this uninitialized/stale owned buffer as the source and can overwrite the earlier buffer's valid contents even though the app only intended to update another aliased/suballocated range. Seed the owned storage from the recorded slice before it becomes the host source.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

In that case the page-rounded capacity after the image should be based on `bound_image_offset + bound_image_size` (and then subtract the offset), otherwise valid `vkMapMemory` ranges can still be rejected. Also, `align64` asserts the alignment is a power of two; it’s safer to guard `page_size` before calling it.

nodes.body: `r300_classic_op_name()` indexes `op_info` without validating that `op` is in-range; passing an invalid enum value would cause an out-of-bounds read and UB. Since this is a public helper, it should defensively handle invalid values.

`r300_classic_op_num_srcs()` indexes `op_info` without validating that `op` is in-range, which can read past the table for invalid values. Returning 0 for unknown ops avoids UB and lets callers fail gracefully.

`r300_classic_instr_append()` uses `op_info[op]` before any validation, so an invalid `op` will crash/UB before the validator can report a useful error. If the design is “validate later”, `append` still needs a simple in-range guard.

`r300_classic_program_validate()` dereferences `p` (and later `p->target`) without checking for NULL, which makes the validator itself crash on malformed input instead of returning a failure + message. Also, OOM in the bitset allocation currently returns false without populating `err`.

The IR claims to reuse RC’s 12-bit swizzle encoding, but the validator currently rejects `RC_SWIZZLE_HALF` (0.5) by treating anything > `RC_SWIZZLE_ONE` as invalid. Existing r300 RC uses `RC_SWIZZLE_HALF` when `has_half_swizzles` is enabled, so this would cause false validation failures once selection starts producing half constants.

`print_swizzle()` maps swizzle selects 6/7 to '?' which makes dumps misleading for valid RC swizzles (notably `RC_SWIZZLE_HALF`, printed as 'H' elsewhere in the r300 compiler). Using the same character mapping as `radeon_program_print.c` keeps dumps consistent and future-proof.

The comment for `swizzle` says the encoding only supports X..W/ZERO/ONE, but RC swizzles also include `RC_SWIZZLE_HALF` (0.5). Since this IR explicitly reuses the RC encoding, the comment should reflect the full set of valid selects.

If `fmemopen()` fails (e.g. runtime error), the test will pass a NULL `FILE*` to `r300_classic_program_print()` and crash instead of reporting a test failure. Adding a simple NULL check keeps the test failure-mode controlled.

`r300_classic_program_validate()` tries to report an “unknown opcode” by calling `fail()`, but `fail()` unconditionally indexes `op_info[i->op]`. For an out-of-range opcode, this makes the validator read past `op_info` while trying to format the error, defeating the point of validation.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Guard unknown opcodes before formatting errors**

When validation sees a malformed instruction with `op >= R300C_OP_COUNT` and the caller supplies an error buffer, this path calls `fail()`, which formats `op_info[i->op].name` before returning. That reads past the opcode table instead of reporting "unknown opcode", so the validator can crash on the very invalid IR it is trying to diagnose.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate swizzles against SSA writemasks**

For SSA sources this only proves that a numeric SSA id was defined earlier; it never checks that the swizzled components are among `src->def->writemask`. A consumer can therefore validate an export such as `t2.yyyy` after the test's scalar `dp3` writes only `t2.x`, letting selection emit reads from undefined temp channels after validation has succeeded.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Replace phase labels with mechanism names**

The repository AGENTS.md says phase terms must not appear in source comments; this new checked-in test comment uses `Phase-1` as the description of the criterion. Please name the mechanism being tested instead, so the comment remains durable if the compiler work is rescheduled or regrouped.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject high writemask bits during validation**

When a value-producing instruction has any bits above `RC_MASK_XYZW` set along with a real channel, validation accepts it because it only checks for at least one low bit. That lets invalid RC masks such as `0x1f` reach the later printer/emitter path, where the extra bit is silently dropped or forwarded as a non-channel write mask instead of being rejected at the IR boundary.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject SSA defs that belong to another program**

This membership check tracks only `ssa_id`, so a source whose `def` pointer comes from a different `r300_classic_program` but has the same dense id as an earlier local instruction validates as if it referenced the local def. Because the IR contract says SSA sources point to the defining instruction in the same program, this can make validation succeed while later passes follow a foreign instruction pointer or misinterpret it as the local temporary.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Enforce texture and KIL source restrictions**

A program can therefore pass the new IR validator and only fail or miscompile when the later RC backend sees an operand shape the hardware path does not support.

nodes.body: `select_tex` stores the texture unit from `tex->texture_index`, but r300’s NIR backend (nir_to_rc) uses `sampler_index` as the unit selection. Using `texture_index` can pick the wrong unit when texture/sampler indices differ (separate textures/samplers or lowered offsets).

The classic IR `R300C_OP_TEX` encoding here only records `tex_unit` and coordinates; it does not preserve sampler dimension/array/shadow semantics. As written, the selector will accept e.g. array/shadow/non-2D samplers and then silently drop that information, producing an incorrect program. Please explicitly reject unsupported sampler shapes until the IR/result carries enough metadata to represent them.

`nir_intrinsic_store_output` selection ignores both `nir_intrinsic_component()` and `nir_intrinsic_write_mask()`. That can silently miscompile partial/component-offset stores (e.g. writing only .zw or only depth.x) by exporting undefined/incorrect channels. If partial exports aren’t supported in this phase, reject them with a named reason rather than ignoring the mask/component.

`r300_classic_select()` documents that it returns `false` only on out-of-memory, but most OOM sites call `reject(ctx, "out of memory")` and then get reported as a normal shader rejection (function returns `true` with `reject_reason`). This hides real allocation failures from callers and violates the API contract in `r300_classic_select.h`. Consider adding an explicit OOM flag/sentinel in `sel_ctx` (or treating `ctx.reject == NULL` as OOM) so OOM can propagate as `return false;`.

This comment claims nir_to_rc does MAD refusion via `nir_opt_algebraic_late`, but the production path actually runs `r300_nir_opt_algebraic_late` (see nir_to_rc.c). Either the selector should run the same pass to truly match shapes, or the comment should be updated so future readers don’t assume it’s bit-for-bit mirroring nir_to_rc’s optimization sequence.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Apply or reject masked output stores**

For `store_output` intrinsics with a nonzero `component` or a partial `nir_intrinsic_write_mask` (for example a shader writing only `gl_FragColor.xy`), this selects the raw `src[0]` and then reports success even though the export IR carries no write-mask/component metadata. The existing `nir_to_rc` path handles the same intrinsics in `ntr_output_decl()`/`ntr_emit_store_output()` by deriving the write mask and reswizzling the source before the MOV; without equivalent handling here, the classic selector can silently produce an export with the wrong channels instead of rejecting the unsupported shape.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Add constant IO offsets to the selected slot**

This treats any nonzero constant IO offset as indirect addressing, but `nir_lower_io()` uses constant offsets for direct array/struct/matrix elements; those should address `base + offset` rather than be rejected as indirect. The current `nir_to_rc` path adds constant offsets in `ntr_emit_load_input()`/`ntr_emit_store_output()` (`ntr_src_offset`/`ntr_dst_offset`), so the new selector will unnecessarily reject otherwise straight-line shaders that read or write a later slot of an IO aggregate.

When `tex->is_array` is true, such as `sampler2DArray` with `texture()`, the source list can still contain only a coordinate after `nir_lower_samplers`, so this check accepts it and emits `R300C_OP_TEX`. The existing `nir_to_rc` texture path explicitly rejects array textures because r300 has no array texture support, and the new classic IR records no array/target bit, so accepting this shape produces an unrepresentable sample instead of the selector's promised named rejection.

If multipass had already produced `shader->multipass_pass_b`, the next attempt can overwrite the pointer and leak the old pass-B code object. Also, when classic selection is used (`classic_done`), the NIR `clone` is still owned by this function (nir_to_rc only takes ownership when it is called), so retrying should free `clone` to avoid leaking one NIR clone per retry.

On the classic-backend retry path after `r3xx_compile_fragment_program` errors, the code frees the current attempt's constants/remap table but still retries without cleaning up `shader->multipass_pass_b` (if multipass splitting happened) or the owned NIR `clone` (classic path doesn't transfer ownership to nir_to_rc). A retry that re-splits will overwrite `multipass_pass_b` and leak the previous pass-B code object.

When `inst_end == -1` and the classic front end was used, the new retry path jumps back to `retry:` without freeing the just-produced code object's constants/remap table. The next compilation attempt will repopulate `shader->code.constants` via `rc_constants_copy` (which assumes an uninitialized destination), so this can leak (and leave stale pointers) across the retry. The same applies to any existing `shader->multipass_pass_b` produced earlier in the attempt, and to the owned NIR `clone`.

Integer-uniform decode currently goes through an intermediate `(int32_t)` cast: `(uint32_t)(int32_t)uif(raw[i])`. Since `r300_inlinable_dw_is_int()` explicitly treats both `nir_type_int` and `nir_type_uint` consumers as integer-consumed, this can invoke undefined behavior for uint-uniform values > INT32_MAX (float-to-signed-int conversion out of range) and mis-handle large unsigned values.

Use a wider signed intermediate (`int64_t`) so all uint32 values produced by the state tracker’s float conversion remain representable during the cast, while still preserving negative signed ints via two’s-complement when cast back to `uint32_t`.

nodes.body:
The loop-nesting guard is incorrect: `nested` is set from `fold_loops_in_cf_list()` which returns whether any *progress* happened in the loop body, not whether the loop body actually contains a nested loop. This means an outer loop that contains a non-foldable inner loop can still be folded, contradicting the comment and potentially violating the pass's intended safety boundary.

Consider explicitly detecting whether `loop->body` still contains any `nir_cf_node_loop` (recursively through ifs) and only running `fold_loop()` when none remain (after attempting to fold inner loops).

`ord` is computed as an LCM of cycle lengths using `unsigned`. For permutations over up to 64 slots, the LCM can overflow 32-bit (and even 64-bit in theory), which can make `steps = trip % ord` incorrect and produce a wrong final swizzle.

Since you only need `trip % ord`, you can safely clamp `ord` once it exceeds `trip` (because then `trip % ord == trip`) and use a wider type during the intermediate multiply.

This pass relies on NIR loop analysis metadata but requests it with `indirect_mask = 0`. That can cause extra loop-analysis reruns later in the same optimization pipeline (e.g., by `nir_opt_loop_unroll`, which requests loop analysis with a nonzero mask) and makes the analysis settings inconsistent with other users (most use `nir_var_all`).

Prefer requesting loop analysis with `nir_var_all` (and the same `force_unroll_sampler_indirect` value you expect) to reduce metadata churn and keep analysis behavior consistent.

New loop-folding behavior is introduced here, but there is no dedicated unit-style coverage under `src/gallium/drivers/r300/compiler/tests/` to guard against regressions (e.g., a small NIR snippet with a counted loop that does `res = res.yzwx` and asserts the loop is eliminated / uses are rewritten).

Given this driver already has a fairly extensive compiler test suite, adding a focused test would make the optimization safer to evolve.

`find_loop_terminators()` only scans `loop->body` top-level CF nodes. As written, this pass walks up through enclosing `nir_cf_node_if` parents, so it can trigger on an `outer` if nested inside another if, insert a new `if (...) break;` in that nested list, and still not make the break visible to terminator discovery. It also makes the function header comment (“so terminator discovery can see it”) untrue for those cases.

Consider requiring that `outer` is an immediate child of a loop (i.e., directly in the loop body list) so the inserted terminator is always discoverable and the transform stays narrowly scoped.
